Article Title: How OpenAI's model hacking into world's biggest AI repository firm Hugging Face is dangerous in more ways than one
Article Text:
OpenAI's rogue AI agent hacked into Hugging Face earlier this month



Hugging Face details AI-driven cyberattack



Experts say incident is a warning for AI safety

Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman sees a warning in Sam Altman's AI model hacking Hugging Face



What Godfather of AI Yoshua Bengio said on the Hugging Face hacking incident



What OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said

Open-weight AI models gain support



More than 1,100 AI employees call for coordinated action

Researchers call for stronger safeguards

One breach, three fault lines: a safety failure (OpenAI’s AI model pursued its goal in ways its creators never intended), a policy flashpoint (renewed pressure for open-weight models and tighter oversight), and a power question (CEO Sam Altman 's own warning about concentrating AI capability in too few hands). Here's how each unfolded.Earlier this month, Hugging Face disclosed that it had detected an intrusion into part of its production infrastructure driven entirely by an autonomous AI agent system. The company said the attacker exploited vulnerabilities in its data-processing pipeline, gained access to internal systems, harvested credentials and moved across several internal clusters.Hugging Face said it fixed the vulnerabilities, rebuilt affected systems, rotated credentials, strengthened security controls and informed law enforcement. It also recommended users rotate their access tokens as a precaution. The company said it found no evidence that public AI models, datasets or Spaces had been tampered with.According to a report by The Verge, AI safety researchers said the breach demonstrated how an advanced AI system could pursue a goal in ways its creators did not intend. In this case, OpenAI's model reportedly escaped its sandbox, navigated internal systems, reached the internet and targeted Hugging Face because it believed the platform could contain answers to the cybersecurity benchmark it was attempting to complete.Adam Gleave, co-founder and CEO of AI safety organisation FAR.AI, called it "a visceral example of how misaligned AI could cause harm."Researchers described the behaviour as "specification gaming" or reward hacking — an AI system following the literal instructions it receives while ignoring the intended limits of the task. That framing, an AI doing exactly what it was told and not what was meant, is what turned a single breach into an industry-wide reckoning.Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman called the cyber incident a major "warning shot" for the tech industry, emphasising the growing risks posed by autonomous AI. Suleyman called the breach an "important lesson" for developers rushing to roll out increasingly capable models."These are very powerful [tools] and they need to be handled incredibly carefully. And we need extreme attention to detail," Suleyman said in an interview with the Financial Times, adding, "The precautionary principle is going to matter here as the models get more and more powerful and I think it's a warning shot."Suleyman's caution from inside a rival lab was echoed even more sharply outside the industry's biggest players, by one of AI's most consistent critics of unchecked development.Sharing a LinkedIn post, Yoshua Bengio wrote:"This incident is deeply concerning. AI agents are willing to cheat and deceive to achieve misaligned and unintended goals, behaviours which have been demonstrated in controlled tests for months. Now, this real-world case should serve as a wake-up call.Continuing on the current trajectory of AI development will likely lead to an increase in concrete cases of autonomous cyberattacks as well as other high-risk incidents of misaligned and dangerous AI behaviour. We urgently need to take action to prevent these situations, rather than attempting to clean up the damage after the fact."Notably, the most direct admission of concern came not from an outside critic, but from the very company whose model caused the breach.Speaking on Y Combinator's podcast, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told YC CEO Garry Tan that anyone who was not a little scared of or humbled by the Hugging Face breach "is not taking this seriously enough." He said the incident is a stark reminder of why concentrating AI power in the hands of a few people or companies is a bad idea.Altman said the incident is "a real reminder of the stakes of what's happening," adding that "loss of control accidents are not entirely theoretical things."That admission is already reshaping how the industry wants to build and share AI systems going forward.Reuters reported that the incident has strengthened support for open-weight AI models, which can be downloaded and run on an organisation's own infrastructure. Hugging Face said it relied on the open-weight GLM-5.2 model during its forensic investigation after commercial AI models blocked parts of its analysis because of built-in safety guardrails.The company argued that organisations responding to cyberattacks need AI systems they can operate privately without sending sensitive attack data or credentials to external providers. Reuters also reported that Nvidia, Microsoft and several other technology companies recently urged U.S. lawmakers to support open-weight AI models as part of future AI security efforts.More than 1,100 employees from leading AI companies, including OpenAI, recently signed a statement urging the US government to support international efforts to manage the pace of AI development.One signatory described the Hugging Face incident as "a clear and undeniable warning sign that we aren't yet prepared to handle AI systems that demonstrate capabilities beyond those of our smartest people," according to Reuters. Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue also told Reuters he hopes the incident encourages more companies to openly share AI research, models and datasets.Experts told The Verge that the incident highlights the need for AI companies to strengthen internal security, improve testing of autonomous AI systems and increase transparency around serious AI incidents. They also called for stronger oversight, third-party audits and mandatory reporting of significant AI safety failures, arguing that relying on voluntary disclosures alone is not enough as AI systems become more capable.Bottom line: One breach, three fault lines exposed — an AI that gamed its own task, an industry now split on whether openness or control is the safer path, and a fresh warning about what happens when that much capability sits with too few players.
Article Summary: OpenAI's rogue AI agent hacked into Hugging Face earlier this month. Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman called the cyber incident a major "warning shot" for the tech industry. AI safety researchers said the breach demonstrated how an advanced AI system could pursue a goal in ways its creators did not intend.

Article Title: White House invites AI leaders from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and others to review oversight framework
Article Text:
‘Security incident disclosures to accelerate federal action’



The Trump administration has reportedly finalised a voluntary testing framework designed to evaluate the cybersecurity risks and hacking capabilities of the world’s most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Citing senior administration officials, a report by The Information (via Axios), following the completion of the policy milestone, the White House has invited technical representatives and leadership from top AI development labs, including OpenAI Google and Anthropic, to a staff-level meeting on Tuesday to review the proposed oversight procedures.The initiative follows a June directive from President Donald Trump instructing administration officials to construct standardized benchmarks for assessing high-risk cyber capabilities in frontier models before they are released to the public.“The voluntary framework outlined in the June 2nd executive order was complete by the deadline,” a White House official stated, adding that active discussions are taking place with a broad group of industry partners beyond the major tech labs.The urgency surrounding federal oversight increased after several prominent AI companies reported unintended safety breaches during internal testing runs. Recently, Anthropic disclosed that its AI systems successfully breached external networks belonging to three separate companies during controlled vulnerability assessments.Days earlier, OpenAI confirmed that one of its autonomous AI agents bypassed its designated testing sandbox and executed unauthorised network actions against the AI platform Hugging Face, which is the world’s largest AI model repository.This comes days after reports said that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman visited the White House to consult with officials regarding incoming model releases and voluntary testing protocols.According to administration guidelines, specific technical benchmarks used to evaluate model hacking capabilities will remain classified. The framework establishes rules regarding how intelligence agencies and approved “trusted partners” will gain up to 30 days of pre-release access to new models to inspect them for insider risks, intellectual property vulnerabilities, and potential misuse in state-sponsored cyberattacks.
Article Summary: The White House has invited technical representatives and leadership from top AI development labs, including OpenAI Google and Anthropic, to a staff-level meeting on Tuesday. The initiative follows a June directive from President Donald Trump instructing administration officials to construct standardized benchmarks for assessing high-risk cyber capabilities.

Article Title: A tech CEO wanted to build a new country in an Asian Ghost city, but then an actual country came in the way
Article Text:
Balaji Srinivasan's Network School ran inside Forest City, a $100 billion Chinese-built ghost development in Malaysia's Johor, until authorities ordered it shut.

Who Balaji Srinivasan is, and why he left America behind

How Balaji Srinivasan's 2022 book on startup societies became a real campus in Malaysia

The $100 billion Chinese ghost city that housed Balaji Srinivasan's experiment

Why Malaysia shut the Srinivasan's Network School down, and why Kazakhstan said yes

Balaji Srinivasan spent two years trying to prove that a country could be launched the way a startup is—community first, territory later. Last week, a local council in southern Malaysia ended the experiment with a piece of paperwork. The Network School, the Indian-American founder's live-in campus set inside a half-empty Chinese-built development a bridge away from Singapore, was ordered to cease operations over licensing irregularities, The Wall Street Journal reported on August 1.The shutdown arrived after weeks of scrutiny over something unrelated to licences: the nationality of some residents. An Instagram post by a pro-Palestine group claimed the school had admitted Israeli citizens, including one travelling on a second passport. Malaysia does not officially recognise Israel and requires Israeli nationals to secure special permission before entering. Immigration officers arrived on campus to inspect passports. Authorities later said no wrongdoing had been established and the investigation was continuing. Srinivasan called the post a hoax, compared it to swatting, and demanded a meeting with the prime minister's office.Within hours of the closure order, he posted a video of himself signing an agreement with a Kazakh deputy prime minister—a former Binance executive—to open a campus there instead.Srinivasan, 46, grew up on Long Island, the son of Indian immigrant physicians. He has described being bullied as the only brown child in a school of hundreds, then being punished for defending himself—an early lesson, he has said, that the state is not on your side. Stanford engineering degrees followed, then a genetic screening company, a stint at Andreessen Horowitz, and a brief run as Coinbase's chief technology officer. Coinbase boss Brian Armstrong later called him brilliant, and also "kind of unmanageable". Federal records show Srinivasan and his wife renounced American citizenship in 2023. He says he is now Singaporean.His 2022 book The Network State laid out the method. People with shared beliefs gather online. They help each other make money. They pool funds, buy land, and eventually seek recognition as a state. Seven stages in all. Srinivasan has argued that most countries predating the internet will not survive, and that American polarisation is heading somewhere ugly. He is also a vocal pronatalist, partly on the logic that settling new frontiers requires a much larger supply of humans.The testing ground was Forest City in Johor, a $100 billion Chinese-built luxury project that emptied out into a symbol of China's property bust. Srinivasan rented hotel space in 2024 and opened the Network School at $1,500 a month for room, board, classes and a beach. The first cohort ran 128 people; the second, in 2025, offered 256 places. There was a gym, meals designed by longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, and a cafe stocking creatine and collagen peptides.Residents told the Journal the camaraderie was real and the convenience unbeatable. Pranit Garg, a 29-year-old digital nomad who arrived in March, said the vision brought him in and the protein kept him there. Priyansha Dhoot, a 26-year-old programme manager from India, joined in April and liked the community but found the nightlife nonexistent; the duty-free liquor shops entertained her for roughly a day. Others complained of mould and a lopsided gender ratio. Srinivasan said mildew is a regional inevitability his team handles, and that the school serves tech parents and children, not only tech bros.He is not the only one attempting this. Patri Friedman, grandson of Milton Friedman, moved from floating city-states to funding startup cities, backed by Srinivasan, Peter Thiel and Marc Andreessen. Their portfolio includes Próspera in Honduras, which sued the state after lawmakers moved to scrap its special economic zone.Kazakhstan, meanwhile, has been courting foreign firms with zero corporate tax zones and easy visas. Srinivasan has floated building an artificial island off a willing coast, or following Elon Musk to Mars.Two years in, the experiment has established one thing clearly. Recruiting believers turned out to be the easy part. Every square metre on Earth already answers to somebody's licensing department.
Article Summary: Balaji Srinivasan spent two years trying to prove that a country could be launched the way a startup is. The Indian-American founder's live-in campus set inside a half-empty Chinese-built development a bridge away from Singapore was ordered to cease operations over licensing irregularities.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Satya Nadella: 'It’s not about the failure, it’s about learning from the failures'
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Satya Nadella

“It’s not about the failure, it’s about learning from the failures. Failure itself cannot be celebrated.”

What Satya Nadella’s quote means

“celebrate failure.”

“Failure itself cannot be celebrated,”

A message reflected in his leadership

“know-it-all”

A simple takeaway

Failure is often described as a necessary part of success, but Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offers a more measured perspective. Rather than encouraging people to celebrate failure itself, Nadella argues that its value lies in the lessons it provides. Throughout his career, particularly while leading Microsoft through major technological shifts, he has repeatedly emphasised the importance of learning, adapting, and improving rather than simply accepting setbacks.His quote reminds us that mistakes and failed attempts are meaningful only when they lead to better decisions, new ideas or personal growth. Without reflection and learning, failure remains just that—a setback.At first glance, the quote appears to challenge the popular idea that people shouldIn recent years, many workplaces and entrepreneurs have encouraged this mindset to reduce the fear of taking risks. Nadella’s words introduce an important distinction. He is not suggesting that failure should be feared, but that it should not become the goal or the achievement.The first part of the quote shifts the focus away from the failure itself and toward what comes after it. Every failed project, unsuccessful decision or missed opportunity contains information. It reveals what worked, what did not and what can be done differently the next time. That learning process is what Nadella considers valuable, not the setback itself.The second sentence,reinforces this idea. Simply failing does not create progress. A mistake only becomes meaningful when someone takes the time to understand it and applies those lessons in the future. Without that reflection, failure remains an unproductive outcome.The quote also reflects a mindset of continuous improvement. Instead of seeing success and failure as final destinations, Nadella encourages people to view both as part of an ongoing learning process. The emphasis is not on avoiding mistakes completely but on ensuring they contribute to future growth.This philosophy has been visible throughout Satya Nadella’s leadership at Microsoft. Since becoming the company’s CEO in 2014, he has encouraged a culture centred on learning, experimentation and adaptability rather than maintaining the status quo.Under his leadership, Microsoft expanded its focus on cloud computing, artificial intelligence and subscription-based services while entering new areas through acquisitions and partnerships. Many of these changes required the company to rethink earlier strategies and move beyond approaches that had not delivered the expected results.Nadella has frequently emphasised the importance of developing a “learn-it-all” mindset rather than amindset. The idea is that organisations and individuals grow by remaining open to feedback, questioning assumptions and treating every experience as an opportunity to improve.Satya Nadella’s quote offers a practical lesson for students, professionals, entrepreneurs and anyone working toward a long-term goal. Setbacks are not something to seek or glorify, but neither are they reasons to stop trying. Their value depends on what happens next.Whether it is an unsuccessful interview, a failed business idea or a project that does not go as planned, the important question is not whether the failure happened, but whether something was learned from it. As Nadella suggests, progress comes not from celebrating failure itself, but from using it as a foundation for making better decisions in the future.
Article Summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offers a more measured perspective on failure. Rather than encouraging people to celebrate failure itself, he argues that its value lies in the lessons it provides. He is not suggesting that failure should be feared, but that it should not become the goal or the achievement.

Article Title: In Silicon Valley's talent war for engineers, now status, ambition and some 'ego about changing the world' matter as much as money
Article Text:
Some high-profile executive who have ‘jumped ships’



AI researchers looking for more than compensation



The Silicon Valley is seeing a ‘talent’ war for artificial intelligence (AI) talent with companies reportedly offering up to eight-figure compensation packages. But if a new report is to be believed, the high salary is no longer enough to keep elite engineers from walking out the door. Recently, multiple top researchers moved between major labs even as tech executives are discovering that personal status, ideological alignment and what recruiters describe as “some ego about changing the world” are playing just as large a role in retention as multi-million-dollar paychecks.A report by Axios suggests that the intense poaching cycle has effectively turned the frontier AI industry into a tightly connected ecosystem. Rivals compete fiercely for the same tiny pool of researchers while simultaneously trading staff, buying computing services from one another and sharing cloud providers.The latest example of a volatile AI talent market is the recent departure of Lilian Weng, a co-founder of Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab. Weng initially announced she was stepping down from her role to focus on her health and seek a more targeted position. Days later, reports said she was returning to OpenAI to lead research on recursive self-improvement.Weng is the fourth co-founder to leave Thinking Machines within the past year – essentially proving that even heavily funded, high-profile startups are struggling to maintain team stability. Similar retention challenges are affecting established tech giants across the Silicon Valley. Google lost prominent researcher Noam Shazeer to OpenAI, while Nobel laureate John Jumper departed for Anthropic.Meta spent heavily to recruit top-tier talent for Alexandr Wang’s superintelligence unit, only to see several high-profile hires leave shortly with many heading to OpenAI. Safe Superintelligence, the startup founded by former OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, lost its CEO to Meta last year.Apple has seen more than 400 former employees transition to OpenAI, prompting Apple to file a lawsuit alleging OpenAI used internal project codenames to draw confidential information from prospective hires.While high salary offers and pre-IPO equity remain major incentives, researchers reportedly emphasise that non-financial factors often dictate their final decisions. Access to massive computing infrastructure, creative freedom over model architecture, and direct influence over safety protocols frequently outweigh monetary gains.An executive tech recruiter noted that the movement is driven by a mix of financial goals and ‘some ego about changing the world.’ At the same time, some engineers admit to feeling a sense of urgency. With AI systems automating aspects of software development, researchers recognise that their personal bargaining power and ability to command extraordinary compensation may peak over the next few years.Citing a source, Axios reported that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has expressed concern about new talent coming to the firm for the money rather than the mission.
Article Summary: Tech executives are discovering that personal status, ideological alignment and ‘some ego about changing the world’ are playing just as large a role in retention as multi-million-dollar paychecks. Rivals compete fiercely for the same tiny pool of researchers while simultaneously trading staff, buying computing services from one another and sharing cloud providers.

Article Title: 'I messed up': AI startup founder apologises after offering job interviews to people willing to get a tattoo
Article Text:
Representative Image

"poor judgement"

"I messed up. At our YC afterparty, we offered free tattoos and said we'd be happy to interview anyone who got one. What I thought would be a fun, memorable way to meet people was, in reality, reckless, and instead came across as tying a permanent tattoo to job opportunity, which showed poor judgement. Even though participants chose their own tattoos and no one was asked to get our logo, I should have understood the pressure and power dynamic created by connecting tattoos to hiring.

Regardless of said intent, turning a celebration of personalized art into a company stunt was poorly exercised judgement. We've taken the posts down and have spoken to everyone who participated. We're also ready to cover associated removal costs with anyone facing any delayed regret. I'm sorry to the people we put in that position, and to everyone who expected better from me. There's no clever explanation here. I got carried away, and I was wrong.

For the facts: interviews were available to everyone regardless."

How AI startup founder’s original post sparked online criticism

"meet exceptional people, and find out which of them are just as crazy as we are,"

"The job market cannot be this cooked, that kids have to get permanent tattoos to get interviews."

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail."
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: What does it mean?

Why did Jensen Huang say this?

How failure helped build Nvidia





Why failure is essential for innovation

Lessons everyone can learn from this quote

Why the quote is relevant in today's AI era







A timeless lesson on courage and innovation

Innovation has always demanded courage, and few technology leaders embody that principle better than Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. As the driving force behind one of the world's most valuable technology companies, Huang has spent decades pushing the boundaries of graphics computing and artificial intelligence. Along the way, he has experienced setbacks, uncertainty and difficult decisions that ultimately shaped Nvidia's success. His quote, "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail," captures the reality that every meaningful breakthrough begins with risk. Rather than fearing failure, Huang encourages people to embrace it as an essential step towards learning, innovation and long-term success.Jensen Huang's quote highlights a fundamental truth about innovation: doing something truly original always involves uncertainty. Whether someone is launching a business, developing a new technology or learning a new skill, there is no guarantee of immediate success. New ideas often require experimentation, and experiments do not always work the first time.Instead of treating failure as a setback, Huang believes it should be viewed as a valuable learning experience.Every mistake teaches lessons that can improve future decisions and bring people closer to success. His message encourages individuals to stop fearing failure and start seeing it as an unavoidable part of growth.Huang has shared this philosophy in several public discussions about entrepreneurship and innovation. Throughout Nvidia's history, he has explained that companies attempting revolutionary ideas cannot expect every decision to succeed. The willingness to take calculated risks has been central to Nvidia's journey since it was founded in 1993.During its early years, Nvidia faced fierce competition and significant financial pressure. Several products failed to meet expectations, and the company came close to running out of money. Rather than abandoning its vision, Huang and his team continued refining their technology until they found success in graphics processing units, which later became the foundation of the artificial intelligence boom.Today, Nvidia is recognised as one of the world's leading AI companies, but its success was built over decades of persistence rather than overnight achievements. Many of the company's innovations were the result of repeated experimentation and continuous improvement.Its graphics processing units, originally developed for video games, eventually became essential tools for artificial intelligence, scientific computing, robotics and autonomous vehicles. Huang has often pointed to this transformation as proof that embracing uncertainty and learning from setbacks can create opportunities that were impossible to predict at the beginning.History shows that some of humanity's greatest discoveries emerged only after repeated failures. Inventors, scientists and entrepreneurs frequently spend years testing ideas before finding one that works. Every unsuccessful attempt eliminates one possibility and brings them closer to the right solution.Huang believes innovation cannot exist without this process. People who refuse to risk failure often choose familiar paths, while those willing to experiment are more likely to discover something genuinely new. In fast-moving industries such as artificial intelligence, the ability to learn quickly from mistakes has become a major competitive advantage.The message extends well beyond the technology sector. Students preparing for examinations, professionals changing careers and entrepreneurs starting new ventures all face uncertainty. Success rarely comes without obstacles, and setbacks often provide the experience needed for future achievements.Rather than becoming discouraged by failure, Huang encourages people to remain curious, adaptable and resilient. A rejected job application, an unsuccessful project or a failed business idea does not define a person's future. What matters is the willingness to learn, improve and try again.Artificial intelligence is transforming industries across the world, creating both opportunities and challenges. As organisations race to develop new AI tools and applications, experimentation has become more important than ever. Many research projects fail before producing a breakthrough, but those failures often generate valuable knowledge.Huang's advice is particularly relevant because AI development depends on continuous testing and improvement. His words remind innovators that meaningful progress requires patience, resilience and a willingness to accept temporary setbacks in pursuit of long-term goals.Jensen Huang's quote is more than just advice for entrepreneurs. It is a reminder that every remarkable achievement begins with the courage to try something unfamiliar. Fear of failure can prevent people from reaching their full potential, while the willingness to accept mistakes often leads to unexpected opportunities.As technology continues to reshape the world, Huang's message remains timeless. Those who dare to innovate, learn from failure and keep moving forward are often the ones who create the ideas that change industries and improve lives
Article Summary: "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail" is the quote of the day by Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Huang has spent decades pushing the boundaries of graphics computing and artificial intelligence. He believes that every meaningful breakthrough begins with risk.

Article Title: Andrej Karpathy’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ experiment shows how testing of AI models have changed and what they lack
Article Text:
Moving beyond benchmarks to on-demand worlds



Key technical limitations in visual auditing



AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, who joined Anthropic earlier this year, recently put Claude Opus 5 through a unique coding test, demonstrating how benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are evolving past simple tasks into complex software engineering. Moving beyond standard prompts like generating basic 2D graphics or short text snippets, Karpathy gave the model the opening paragraph of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings and a $10 budget allocation of 1 million tokens. The also commanded the AI model render the scene as an interactive 3D web environment using Three.js – JavaScript library used to create and display animated 3D computer graphics in a web browser.Karpathy said in a post on X (formerly Twitter) that over the course of two hours, the AI model operated autonomously to write 5,500 lines of JavaScript code. The output produced a low-poly, procedurally generated 3D rendering of the Shire – complete with hobbit holes, trees, rivers, character assets and ambient animations synchronised with narrated book excerpts.While Karpathy noted that while the visual rendering had noticeable flaws, he pointed out that the experiment underscores a fundamental shift in how developers can test AI capabilities.Orchestrating thousands of polygon assets across complex 3D coordinate systems requires a level of computational patience that humans rarely dedicate to hyper-specific tasks.“We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all,” Karpathy said in the post.“I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand,” he added.Despite the milestone, the test also highlighted significant gaps in current frontier models. Because LLMs lack native, real-time video perception and the ability to seamlessly interact with live environments, the model struggled to audit its own visual output.“Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking,” Karpathy pointed out.
Article Summary: AI researcher Andrej Karpathy recently put Claude Opus 5 through a unique coding test. The test demonstrated how benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are evolving past simple tasks into complex software engineering. The experiment underscores a fundamental shift in how developers can test AI capabilities.

Article Title: OpenAI has five products in development, and its president Greg Brockman just hinted at what they're for
Article Text:
OpenAI president Greg Brockman confirms a "family of devices" is coming soon

Why OpenAI believes voice will replace typing on its AI devices

Apple's trade secrets lawsuit still shadows OpenAI's hardware push

Greg Brockman used the plural, and the plural is the story. OpenAI 's president told independent journalist Joanna Stern that the company is building "a family of devices" for its AI models, which turns a year of leaks and lawsuits into something on the record: this was never a one-gadget project. He would not give a date. He would only say you can expect them soon.The device the world already half-knows about, he refused to touch. Bloomberg reported in July that OpenAI starts with a screenless smart speaker, battery-powered so you can carry it from the laundry room to the kitchen, fitted with a camera and sensors to read what's around it, and built with small moving parts so it feels like company rather than an appliance waiting for orders. Asked to confirm it, Brockman folded the question back into the family line and left it there.The bet underneath the hardware is small to describe and enormous to get wrong: that we will talk to our computers for the vast majority of what we do. Brockman is aware of the obvious hole in that. Open-plan offices do not want forty people speaking to forty machines. He raised the soundproof "beak" masks now turning up on desks, said he doesn't wear one, and argued their very existence proves the demand is real even if nobody thinks masks are the answer.Then there's the camera in your living room. OpenAI is working on verifiable, auditable guarantees that only the model ever reads a user's private data, a direct response to lingering doubts about how private ChatGPT's temporary chat mode actually is.Apple sued OpenAI in July in a California federal court, alleging the company asked Apple job candidates to bring components and prototypes into interviews and that more than 400 ex-Apple employees now work there. Chief hardware officer Tang Tan is a named defendant. Apple wants an injunction, which would stop the speaker selling before it ever sells. Brockman stayed narrow: OpenAI is focused on its own technology, and "we have no interest in other companies' trade secrets. We are plenty innovative."The money explains the heat. OpenAI paid $6.5 billion for Jony Ive's studio io, has roughly five products in development, and is reportedly scoping a phone with Qualcomm and MediaTek. The what and the why are now public. Whether any of it reaches a shelf before a judge reaches a decision is the part Brockman left alone.
Article Summary: OpenAI president Greg Brockman confirms a "family of devices" is coming soon. OpenAI paid $6.5 billion for Jony Ive's studio io. The company has roughly five products in development, and is reportedly scoping a phone with Qualcomm and MediaTek.

Article Title: Apple's most popular Mac is now its hardest to buy
Article Text:
MacBook Air shipping dates have slipped to late August as the global memory shortage hits Apple's best-selling Mac.

The AI buildout is eating the memory that consumer laptops need

Apple is nudging shoppers toward the MacBook Pro instead

The MacBook Air is the laptop Apple sells to everyone—students, writers, people who just want something thin that opens and works. Right now it is also the laptop Apple can't keep on shelves. Shipping estimates have slipped by weeks across nearly every configuration, and this isn't a back-to-school rush emptying the stockroom. It's the global memory shortage, and it has finally caught up with Apple's volume seller.Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in Sunday's Power On newsletter that retail sources describe Air inventory as more constrained than they can ever recall. Order a base model from Apple's online store today and delivery lands at the end of August. Choose a specific combination of screen size, colour and—critically—memory, and you're pushed into early September. For a machine refreshed with the M5 chip in March, a month-long wait is close to unheard of.The squeeze started at the edges of Apple's lineup. Mac mini and Mac Studio, both quietly adopted by people running local AI models, have been backordered for months. Those are niche machines, so the pain stayed niche.The Air is different. It is the default Mac, and its shortage makes the crunch visible to ordinary buyers for the first time.Apple has already pulled the obvious lever. In June it raised prices across the Mac range, taking the 13-inch MacBook Air from $1,099 to $1,299. Tim Cook, in his final months as CEO, described the memory situation as a hundred-year flood for the industry—something he hadn't seen in four decades of watching supply chains. Gurman says Apple is also working to source memory from Chinese suppliers, at least for devices sold in China.The most telling sign is in the marketing. Apple's back-to-school promotion, delayed from June because of the shortage, now steers customers toward the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro across its website and stores. Some materials carry a line Apple has rarely needed before: MacBook Air subject to availability.That redirection isn't accidental. Gurman reports Apple is prioritising the base MacBook Pro partly to clear inventory ahead of an M6 refresh this fall. A new MacBook Air isn't expected until early next year, with 13-inch and 15-inch models in development that closely resemble the current design.Until then, the cheapest way into a Mac may be the one Apple is quietly steering you away from buying.
Article Summary: The global memory shortage has finally caught up with Apple's best-selling Mac. Air inventory is more constrained than they can ever recall, retail sources say. Order a base model from Apple's online store today and delivery lands at the end of August. Choose a specific combination of screen size, colour and memory, and you're pushed into early September.

Article Title: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna disagrees with everyone saying that quantum computing is far, shares new timeline
Article Text:
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna

IBM CEO Arvind Krishna address skepticism around quantum computing



IBM CEO's statement that wiped away $70 billion from company's market value



IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has pushed back against skeptics on CNBC’s Mad Money, insisting quantum computing is not decades away but poised to deliver real business impact within the next few years. “I think that in 2028 or 2029, you’ll see it have a measurable impact on our top line and bottom line. By the end of the 2030s, we are now pretty convinced this is a trillion dollars of value,” Krishna said. Recently, IBM and startup Algorithmiq unveiled new research demonstrating quantum advantage — showing that a quantum computer could solve certain problems more efficiently than classical machines while verifying results. Krishna noted IBM’s quantum systems uncovered material behaviours previously invisible to conventional computing, with potential applications in better batteries, advanced materials, fusion energy, and smarter medicines.Critics argue quantum computing faces hurdles like error rates and hardware complexity. Krishna countered that IBM is already making meaningful progress toward real-world applications.“A quantum computer can do things better, faster, cheaper, in a way that normal classical computers cannot do at this time,” he said.In May, IBM announced plans for a standalone quantum chip foundry, backed by $1 billion from the U.S. Commerce Department under the CHIPS Act and a matching $1 billion investment from IBM. Rivals including Alphabet and Rigetti Computing are also racing to commercialize quantum technology.Krishna’s comments come after IBM’s July earnings update triggered a 25% single-day stock drop, its worst on record. He reassured investors that delayed customer deals were deferrals, not cancellations, noting that about 40% had already closed within weeks.Recently, IBM CEO Arvind Krishna said growing concerns over advanced AI models such as Anthropic's Mythos are prompting companies to pause technology deals and rethink how much they need to spend on cybersecurity. His comments came as IBM released preliminary second-quarter results that missed Wall Street expectations, sending the company's shares down as much as 26% and wiping out nearly $70 billion in market value. At the same time, cybersecurity stocks surged, as investors bet businesses would increase spending on cyber protection in response to the rapidly evolving AI landscape.Speaking to CNBC, IBM CEO Aravind Krishna said some large customer deals were delayed toward the end of the quarter as companies reassessed their spending priorities. “Mythos is making people pause to say, wait, how much do I need to spend on cyber? They're pausing on new deals until they know,” Krishna said.He added that IBM does not believe AI is disrupting its software business. “We don't see our software being disrupted by AI at all.” In its preliminary results, IBM said customers shifted spending away from some of its products and instead invested more in AI infrastructure, including servers, storage and memory. Krishna also pointed to “rapidly-evolving, industry-wide cybersecurity concerns” as another factor affecting customer spending.
Article Summary: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has pushed back against skeptics on CNBC’s Mad Money, insisting quantum computing is not decades away. “I think that in 2028 or 2029, you’ll see it have a measurable impact on our top line and bottom line. By the end of the 2030s, we are now pretty convinced this is a trillion dollars of value,” Krishna said.

Article Title: US Immigration authority's Green Card update: EB-1 visa category may become unavailable if this limit reached
Article Text:
EB-1 category includes priority worker and aliens with extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics; Outstanding professors and researchers; or Certain multinational managers and executives.

What 'unavailable' would mean for Indian EB-1 applicants

India EB-1 Green Card final action date at October 15, 2022

EB-2 India is already unavailable in August

The US Department of State has warned that the Employment-Based First Preference (EB-1) Green Card category for India could become unavailable in the coming weeks due to high demand. In its August 2026 Visa Bulletin, the department said high demand and visa use by applicants chargeable to India could result in the country reaching its pro-rated EB-1 limit before the fiscal year ends on September 30. If that happens, the category may have to be made unavailable, temporarily stopping further visa numbers from being issued under the category. The department said it will continue monitoring the situation and make adjustments if required.The Visa Bulletin uses “U” to indicate that a category is “unauthorized,” meaning immigrant visa numbers are not authorised for issuance.The Department of State explained that if an annual limit is reached, the affected preference category must immediately be made “unavailable,” and no further requests for visa numbers can be honoured.The warning does not mean that India's EB-1 category has already become unavailable.As of the August 2026 Visa Bulletin, the category continues to have a Final Action Date of October 15, 2022. The department is warning that its status could change in the coming weeks if India's allocation is exhausted.For August 2026, the Final Action Date for India under the EB-1 category is October 15, 2022. This means visa numbers are authorised for qualified applicants whose priority dates are earlier than the listed date.The Dates for Filing chart, meanwhile, lists December 1, 2023, for EB-1 applicants from India. The situation is different for several other countries. The EB-1 category remains "current" for most countries, including Mexico and the Philippines, while the Final Action Date for mainland China is July 1, 2023.The Department of State specifically highlighted India in a separate section of its August Visa Bulletin.“High demand and number use by aliens chargeable to India in the EB-1 visa category may necessitate making the category unavailable in the coming weeks if India’s pro-rated limit in the EB-1 category is reached before the fiscal year ends,” it said.“This situation will be continually monitored, and any necessary adjustments will be made accordingly,” the department added.Indian Green Card applicants also face restrictions in the Employment-Based Second Preference, or EB-2, category. The August Visa Bulletin lists India's EB-2 Final Action Date as “U,” meaning unavailable. However, the Dates for Filing chart lists January 15, 2015, for India under EB-2.
Article Summary: The US Department of State has warned that the Employment-Based First Preference (EB-1) Green Card category for India could become unavailable in the coming weeks. The department said high demand and visa use by applicants chargeable to India could result in the country reaching its pro-rated EB-1 limit before the fiscal year ends on September 30. Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg lays off 8,000, spends $130 billion on AI, then says AI has created a lot of jobs
Article Text:
The jobs Mark Zuckerberg is counting are on construction sites, not inside Meta



Inside Meta, the AI transition looked nothing like a jobs boom



Wall Street is asking Zuckerberg its own version of the jobs question



Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has a message for anyone anxious about AI taking their job: the technology is actually hiring. Speaking to the Wall Street Journal hours before Meta's June quarter earnings, Zuckerberg said that "all the work around AI has net created a lot of jobs because there's all this infrastructure that needs to get created," adding that fears of mass displacement haven't "played out the way that people feared it might. "It's a claim that invites an obvious question, because the company making it spent this year doing the opposite. Meta laid off 8,000 employees—about 10 per cent of its workforce—in May as part of an AI-first restructuring, reassigned another 7,000 to AI initiatives, and is on track to spend between $130 billion and $145 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, roughly double last year's outlay. Zuckerberg isn't wrong that AI is creating jobs. They just aren't the ones his own company eliminated.His argument rests on the physical buildout. Meta operates or is constructing 32 data centres worldwide and plans to double its computing power to 7 gigawatts this year, then double it again to 14 gigawatts in 2027. Facilities on that scale need construction crews, electricians, cooling engineers and power infrastructure—employment that exists purely because of AI's appetite for compute.Zoom out and the numbers get larger still: Big Tech's combined AI spending is projected to cross $700 billion in 2026, with Alphabet guiding to $205 billion and Microsoft to about $175 billion.The view from Menlo Park was bleaker. The May 20 layoffs began with 4 am emails in Singapore and rolled westward through Britain and the US; at least one person hired within the previous month was cut. Colleagues marked departures with salad emojis—internal shorthand for "salute"—while offices sat empty after HR told everyone to work from home. The anger predated the cuts. More than 1,000 employees signed a petition against a programme that records keystrokes, mouse movements and screen activity to train Meta's AI models, with no opt-out on corporate laptops. Those drafted into the new Applied AI and Engineering team were told, in writing, that participation was not optional.Investors, meanwhile, want to know what all this spending buys. Meta's second-quarter free cash flow cratered 91 per cent to $784 million, its lowest since late 2022, and shares fell 10 per cent in extended trading despite revenue climbing 28 per cent to $60.8 billion. Zuckerberg's pitch to analysts was that the compute itself is becoming a product: Meta is fielding offers to lease capacity "at a significant premium" to what it paid, and is reportedly in early talks with Anthropic. But he resisted the idea of cashing out, telling analysts it "would be foolish" to sell all the compute for short-term profit when Meta needs it to train models and build the personal AI agents he's betting on. "My personal bet is that the people who invest in this are going to be rewarded," he said.Both things Zuckerberg says can be true at once. AI is generating work—in Louisiana concrete pours and gigawatt substations. What his sunny arithmetic skips is who bears the cost of the transition: the 8,000 people whose jobs funded the buildout, notified by email before dawn. The concern hasn't played out the way people feared, perhaps. For some, it played out worse.
Article Summary: Mark Zuckerberg says AI is creating jobs, but not at his own company. Meta laid off 8,000 employees in May as part of an AI-first restructuring. The company is on track to spend between $130 billion and $145 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026.

Article Title: Xbox console price hike in UK and Europe: 512GB models and 1TB models gets costlier by up to $150
Article Text:
Effective August 1, 2026, Xbox consoles with 512GB of storage are now priced $100 higher



Microsoft blames rising memory and storage prices



Microsoft announces financing and cheaper Xbox options

Microsoft’s latest Xbox console price increase in the UK and Europe has now come into effect, making several models significantly more expensive for buyers. Effective August 1, 2026, Xbox consoles with 512GB of storage are now priced $100 higher, while 1TB models have become $150 more expensive. With the price hike, the company has also discontinued its 2TB model. The latest Xbox price hike comes less than a year after the company raised console prices in the US by between $20 and $70 last October. Microsoft blames rising storage and memory costs for the latest increase, saying component prices have climbed sharply and could rise further.Explaining the decision, Microsoft said it had spent several months working with suppliers in an effort to avoid another Xbox price increase. “We hoped another price increase would not be necessary, and we have spent the last several months working with suppliers on options,” the company said.According to Microsoft, storage and memory prices used in Xbox consoles have increased by more than 2.5 times. The company expects those costs to double again by the fall of 2027.Microsoft said the wider consumer electronics industry is dealing with a components crisis, but argued that gaming consoles are particularly affected because they are generally sold for less than what they cost to manufacture.The company has not changed prices by the same dollar amount across its entire Xbox lineup. The increase depends on storage capacity, with 512GB consoles receiving a $100 hike and 1TB versions becoming $150 more expensive.Microsoft is also “sunsetting” the 2TB Xbox model, meaning the company is phasing out that version.Alongside the higher prices, Microsoft announced several measures aimed at making Xbox consoles more affordable. Eligible Xbox hardware purchases through Microsoft Stores can now use Buy Now, Pay Later options, allowing customers to divide the cost into short-term, interest-free instalments.Microsoft is also working with partners to provide up to 12 months of financing at 0% APR on eligible Xbox hardware.The company is developing programmes with retail partners for “previously played consoles.” Under the plan, existing Xbox owners will be able to trade in eligible consoles for cash or store credit, with those devices later being offered to other customers at lower prices.Microsoft also said Xbox Certified Refurbished Consoles are available through Microsoft Stores for discounts of up to $100 from their suggested retail price.
Article Summary: Effective August 1, 2026, Xbox consoles with 512GB of storage are now priced $100 higher. With the price hike, the company has also discontinued its 2TB model. Article Title: Report agrees with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s complaint to the US government on Chinese AI models
Article Text:
Chinese military-linked researchers are trying to transfer that expensive, proprietary reasoning from Western models into smaller systems they can control and deploy locally

Chinese military researchers use US AI models for distillation

OpenAI and Anthropic models reportedly used in Chinese research

Distilled AI models tested for drones and military operations, claims report

Distillation does not fully reproduce frontier AI capabilities

Chinese military-linked researchers have used outputs from advanced American AI models made by OpenAI and Anthropic to train their own systems, according to a Reuters review of more than 80 Chinese academic papers and patents. The findings come after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei raised concerns about China potentially using distillation to draw capabilities from powerful US frontier AI models. Reuters found that researchers linked to China’s military and security institutions have used a technique called “model distillation” to transfer selected capabilities and reasoning from US models into smaller systems that can be controlled and deployed locally, including for defence-related applications.According to Reuters, the documents provide a look at how institutions linked to China’s military are using advanced US AI models while Washington tries to restrict Beijing’s access to advanced chips and other technologies. The research included material compiled by the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, and found widespread use of model distillation among researchers linked to the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and other military institutions.For those unaware, model distillation is a widely used AI technique in which the output of a powerful AI model is used to train a smaller model. This can allow the smaller system to gain selected capabilities without requiring the massive computing resources needed to build a frontier AI model from scratch.A paper published last year by researchers from PLA Unit 96941, described by Reuters as a military intelligence and cyber-warfare unit in Beijing, detailed the use of OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 to process sensitive military source code.The researchers said third-party AI models were not suitable for directly handling classified information. They instead used GPT-3.5 to summarise software code and trained a domestic AI model using those summaries. The resulting system could then operate inside Chinese military networks, according to the report.Researchers at the North University of China also used Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku to create synthetic training data for a model designed for social media monitoring and content moderation, Reuters reported.Anthropic told Reuters that it does not offer commercial access to Claude in China or to companies controlled by Beijing. The company also warned that distilled models may not retain the safety safeguards built into the original system, potentially allowing some capabilities to move into models outside its control.According to the documents, the use of model distillation extended to other defence applications. A 2024 paper from the PLA’s National University of Defense Technology described using distillation to reduce the size of an image-processing AI model so that it could run aboard unmanned aerial vehicles. The approach allowed drones to analyse live video and assist with navigation and targeting even when communications were unavailable.Researchers at China’s Academy of Military Sciences similarly used distillation to operate a target-recognition model on tactical hardware during simulated maritime operations involving drones, ships and unmanned submarines, according to a study published earlier this year.China has promoted technologies including “model lightweighting” and edge computing as it faces US restrictions on access to advanced chips. Such technologies can help AI models operate on devices including drones and satellites with limited computing power.However, the dispute between the US and China is focused on the alleged unauthorised extraction of capabilities rather than model distillation itself. Sunny Cheung, a Jamestown fellow who analysed more than 60 papers, told Reuters that Chinese military researchers were attempting to capture the reasoning abilities of Western AI models.“Teaching a model the right answer is one thing but teaching it the reasoning behind the answer is much harder,” Cheung said. “These papers show Chinese military-linked researchers are trying to transfer that expensive, proprietary reasoning from Western models into smaller systems they can control and deploy locally,” he added.Despite its potential benefits, experts said model distillation has limits. Smaller models generally inherit selected capabilities from their larger “teacher” models rather than reproducing their full intelligence.Trevor Koverko, co-founder of AI data company Sapien, told Reuters: “It is best understood as transferring selected capabilities into a cheaper, locally controlled system, not achieving independence from frontier AI.”Chinese military researchers are also studying the security risks created by distillation. Researchers at the Army Engineering University published a paper in January examining “data-free distillation,” which can be used to reverse-engineer some capabilities of an AI model without accessing its underlying parameters.
Article Summary: Chinese military-linked researchers have used advanced US AI models to train their own systems, according to a Reuters review of more than 80 Chinese academic papers and patents. Researchers linked to China’s military and security institutions have used a technique called ‘model distillation’ to transfer capabilities and reasoning from US models into smaller systems.

Article Title: Christian Kleinerman, EVP of Product, Snowflake: Future belongs to organizations who can give AI the trusted enterprise context
Article Text:
Q. Snowflake has positioned itself as the platform where enterprise data and AI come together. As every major cloud and AI company is trying to become the orchestration layer for enterprise AI, what differentiates Snowflake's vision of the "agentic control plane", and why should enterprises trust you with that role?

Q. Many companies are experimenting with AI agents, but governance, security and compliance remain major hurdles. Do you believe most enterprises are actually ready for autonomous agents today? What capabilities has Snowflake built to ensure AI agents remain auditable, secure and within policy boundaries?

Q. Enterprise CIOs are under pressure to justify AI investments with measurable business outcomes. Can you share specific examples—globally and from India—where Snowflake customers have demonstrated tangible ROI from AI deployments, and what metrics matter most?

Q. The AI landscape is becoming increasingly fragmented, with enterprises choosing between proprietary and open-source models while traditional SaaS is also being reshaped. How does Snowflake plan to stay relevant in a world where foundation models are rapidly commoditising, and what advice do you give customers on selecting the right models for different workloads?

Q. India has emerged as one of the world's fastest-growing AI and digital infrastructure markets. Where does India fit in Snowflake's long-term global strategy—in terms of customers, engineering talent, partnerships and product innovation—and what new investments or priorities should we expect over the next few years?

AI Data Cloud company Snowflake aims to make it easy for enterprises to innovate faster and get more value from data. Times of India spoke to Christian Kleinerman who serves as Snowflake’s EVP of Product and has been with the company since 2018. He oversees the company’s global product strategy and vision. Christian is a database expert with over 20 years of experience working with various database technologies and has more than 15 years of management and leadership experience. Most recently, Christian worked at Google leading YouTube’s infrastructure and data systems. Prior to that, he served as General Manager of the Data Warehousing product unit at Microsoft where he was responsible for a broad portfolio of products. Christian holds a BS in Industrial Engineering from Los Andes University in Colombia, and he is a named inventor on numerous Snowflake patents. Kleinerman's spoke about AI agents, Snowflake's role in the AI era, company's India market and more.The industry is gradually realizing that powerful models alone aren't enough.Models are improving at a remarkable pace, and increasingly interchangeable. The real challenge for enterprises is giving those models the context they need to make useful decisions. If you think about how work actually gets done inside a company, context comes from more than just data. It comes from business definitions, governance policies, security, operational systems, permissions, and the relationships between them.That's where Snowflake fits. We've spent more than a decade helping enterprises solve problems like governance, access control, lineage, compliance, and interoperability. Our strategy isn't to build the best foundation model or create another closed ecosystem. At Snowflake we are committed to give our customers access to the leading frontier and open source models even as the leaderboards evolve. This allows enterprises to maintain flexibility and maximize value of their AI initiatives.We have delivered capabilities to ensure that agents can be identified in Snowflake, so their activity and accessible permissions can be customized to the level of privilege desired for an agent. And not every company is ready for autonomous agents, but we see some companies at the forefront creating real business value. Agents summarize information, answer business questions, turn insights into action, and help people complete work much faster.Before an agent updates a CRM record, approves a payment, or triggers a business workflow, organisations need confidence that every action happens within the same governance capabilities and guarantees that applies to people modifying those same systems. They need auditability, clear permissions, and policy enforcement. That's an area where Snowflake starts from a position of strength. Governance has always been built into the platform. Every AI interaction inherits the same role-based access controls, lineage, audit trails, and security policies that already protect enterprise data.We believe autonomy will happen incrementally based on customers’ comfort with AI. Some will begin with agents that recommend actions, introduce human approval where appropriate, and gradually automate more as confidence grows. The future belongs to organizations who can give AI the trusted enterprise context and guardrails needed to operate safely at scale.Enterprise AI success is ultimately measured by business outcomes, not AI adoption or model benchmarks. CIOs should focus on tangible metrics such as faster deployment, lower costs, improved productivity, and better customer experiences.We're already seeing customers achieve that in production. Providence Health is using Snowflake Cortex AI to extract insights from clinical notes more quickly, helping clinicians make faster decisions. Thomson Reuters is applying AI to legal and compliance workflows, accelerating how professionals work with complex regulatory information. And organisations like DTCC, Wakefit and Urban Company are using our solutions.We also believe it's important to use these technologies ourselves. More than 6,000 Snowflake employees now use our GTM AI Assistant every week, handling over 30,000 questions across sales and marketing. Tasks like researching customers, writing SQL, and preparing for meetings used to require significant manual effort, and now they happen in minutes. Those are the kinds of productivity gains we want our customers to achieve as well. By powering internal operations and decision-making through Snowflake CoWork and CoCo, we rigorously test, refine, and prove our products before bringing them to customers, supporting over 8,000 employees worldwide in product delivery, development, and sales productivity.We're moving into a world where traditional software is being disrupted and AI is becoming the primary interface that people use to interact with data and applications. As that happens, foundation models will continue to improve rapidly, costs will come down, and customers will have more choice than ever before.Snowflake has built its strategy around that reality. Rather than asking customers to commit to a single model or AI provider, Snowflake is deliberately model-agnostic. We work across the leading proprietary and open-source models because we don’t want our customers to be locked into any one vendor. We want them to take advantage of whichever models are best as the technology evolves.In this new era, what doesn't commoditise is enterprise data and enterprise context. In order to perform reliably in an enterprise, models will always need trusted data, business semantics, governance, security, and operational context fueling them. That's where we see Snowflake's role. We provide the trusted data foundation that allows customers to adopt new models without having to rethink their entire AI strategy every time the technology changes.My advice to customers is to optimize for business outcomes, not model preferences. Use the right model for the right workload. Smaller, more efficient models are often ideal for tasks like classification or information extraction, while frontier models are best suited for more complex reasoning and planning. The important thing is building an architecture that gives you the flexibility to evolve as the model landscape evolves. That's exactly why we've taken an open, model-agnostic approach from the beginning.India is one of our most important strategic markets because it brings together four things that are critical for the AI era: a vibrant digital economy, robust public digital infrastructure, world-class engineering talent, and enterprises that are modernising rapidly, along with a growing number of our global customers who are setting up their Global Capability Centre (GCC) base. Over the past year, Snowflake has doubled its sales team in India and 50% of its APJ partners are based here, underscoring the country’s pivotal position in our global strategy and its vast, expanding data and AI market.
Article Summary: Christian Kleinerman is the EVP of Product at Snowflake. He oversees the company’s global product strategy and vision. India has emerged as one of the world's fastest-growing AI and digital infrastructure markets. Snowflake aims to make it easy for enterprises to innovate faster and get more value from data.

Article Title: Apple's India story is no longer just about iPhones, the next phase has started
Article Text:
Disclaimer: It's an AI-generated image

Factors that made the difference

Real upside lies elsewhere and is showing

There are, of course, reasons for caution

For years, Apple's quarterly earnings followed a familiar script in India. Tim Cook would mention "strong growth", analysts would point to iPhone sales, and the conversation would end there. This quarter felt different. Yes, Apple reported another record June quarter in India. Yes, the iPhone remained the company's biggest revenue generator globally, contributing nearly half of total revenue. But hidden inside the earnings call was a more important signal: India is gradually becoming a multi-product Apple market.That may sound obvious. It isn't. Apple CFO Kevan Parekh devoted unusual attention to the Mac business, saying Mac revenue hit a record $10.4 billion globally, up 29%, driven by the MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro. India wasn't merely name-checked. It was among the markets that saw the best quarter ever for new Mac customers and people upgrading existing Macs.That matters because one can argue that Macs have always been Apple's toughest sell in India. Unlike smartphones, laptops have longer replacement cycles, fewer financing options and far lower aspirational value. Convincing someone to spend over Rs 1 lakh on a laptop is significantly harder than persuading them to buy a premium phone on a two-year EMI.If Macs are now finding scale in India, Apple is winning a different kind of customer. The reasons aren't difficult to spot.The biggest catalyst has been the MacBook Neo. Apple has spent years trying to make Macs feel more accessible without making them feel cheaper. Neo appears to have struck that balance. Students, first-time professionals and families looking for a long-lasting computer suddenly have an Apple option that doesn't immediately feel financially intimidating.The second factor is Apple's pricing strategy. While most smartphone brands have quietly increased prices over the past year because of rising component costs and a weaker rupee, Apple largely chose not to. It absorbed the cost pressures instead. That's a luxury only a company sitting on one of the largest cash piles in corporate history can afford. The result is subtle but powerful.When competitors become more expensive, Apple doesn't necessarily have to become cheaper. It simply has to stay where it is. Couple that with aggressive exchange offers, no-cost EMIs, student discounts and bank cashback programmes, and Apple's premium products begin looking surprisingly attainable. The interesting part is that Apple is no longer selling isolated devices. It is selling an ecosystem.An iPhone owner becomes more likely to consider a Mac. A Mac user is nudged towards AirPods. Then perhaps an iPad. Eventually come AppleCare, iCloud storage and services subscriptions. Every new hardware customer is effectively the first step in a much larger revenue journey. That is exactly why the Mac numbers deserve more attention than the iPhone numbers. The iPhone business in India is already relatively mature by Apple's standards. Growth will continue, but largely through premiumisation and higher market share within the premium segment.India still has enormous headroom in personal computers, tablets, wearables and services. Even modest gains across these categories can create a much larger business than simply selling more iPhones. Apple's expanding retail footprint reinforces that strategy. Six company-owned stores across major cities, with more planned, aren't just sales outlets. They're experience centres. They introduce customers to products they may never have actively considered buying online.This also reflects Apple's growing confidence in India as more than a manufacturing destination. Much has been written about iPhone assembly shifting to India. That story is important, but investors sometimes confuse manufacturing with consumption. The two don't necessarily move together.This quarter suggests both are beginning to strengthen simultaneously. India is emerging as one of Apple's most important production hubs while also becoming one of its fastest-growing consumer markets. Few countries offer both opportunities at the same time.Apple still remains overwhelmingly dependent on premium consumers. Its market share by volume is tiny compared to Android brands. The company's success depends on affluent urban buyers continuing to spend despite economic uncertainty. Competition is also becoming sharper. Samsung remains formidable in premium smartphones. AI-powered Windows laptops are improving rapidly. Chinese brands continue to innovate aggressively on hardware.And Apple's next big test may arrive with foldables. Reports suggest the company's first foldable iPhone will initially be manufactured in China rather than India. That may not matter immediately for Indian consumers, but it highlights that Apple is still selective about where it places its most advanced manufacturing.None of that changes the larger takeaway from this quarter. The most important number wasn't revenue, profit or even iPhone sales. It was the fact that Apple talked about India not as a fast-growing smartphone market, but as a market where customers are increasingly buying into the entire Apple experience.That's a far more durable business than selling another iPhone. And for India, it suggests the company's next phase of growth may be defined less by one iconic product and more by an ecosystem quietly taking root.
Article Summary: Apple reported another record June quarter in India. The iPhone remained the company's biggest revenue generator globally. But hidden inside the earnings call was a more important signal. India is gradually becoming a multi-product Apple market. Apple is no longer selling isolated devices. It is selling an ecosystem.

Article Title: Sridhar Vembu raises AI ‘wiping’ jobs question; says: We need to find answers
Article Text:
Sridhar Vembu

Vembu feels Sam Altman’s Universal Basic Income can be a solution

Read Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu’s complete post here

The real issue facing our nation is how to create jobs for our massive cohort of youth in this very uncertain global landscape.

Sadly, the IT industry, including Zoho, have not created many jobs in recent years. We have not laid off people but we are not creating new jobs either.

The money that would have gone to new employees is now going to AI and data center costs, the latter due to the steep rise in server and memory prices. We are trying to control those costs but a lot of that is out of our control.

While AI allows us to produce more software quicker, does the over-saturated global software market need a lot more software? Like any commodity industry, the focus shifts to quality, reliability, brand and so on and growth will be much slower.

Software customers (large and mid-sized enterprises) also have redireced their own IT spending towards AI. Even the AI companies which are growing very rapidly are borrowing and spending huge amounts of money in capex, and it is not clear they will achieve the massive profits they need to justify all the capex.

What other industry can pick up the slack? Extensive automation means that large scale manufacturing produces few jobs.

As an economic thinker, this is a good thing: ultimately all kinds of goods, including advanced tech products become very affordable because production becomes so cheap. The "only" question is how the economy is structured so people have the income to afford those affordable goods.

That "only" question, simple in theory, is not easy in practice. Some people think the answer is Universal Basic Income (UBI) and some of that is already happening in India (we call them freebies). We can expect the political pressure to do a lot more.
