Is there a better answer? Continued ...

Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu has publicly raised concerns about artificial intelligence ‘wiping’ jobs, warning that India must urgently find answers to safeguard its massive youth workforce. In a post shared on social media platform X(formerly known as Twitter) Vembu mentioned that the real issue facing the nation right now is how to create jobs in an uncertain global landscape, noting that the IT industry including Zoho has not generated any significant new employment in the recent years. Vembu further explained that money which was once earmarked for new employees is now being spent on AI and rising data center costs, driven by steep increases in server and memory prices. He further noted that while Zoho has avoided layoffs, but admitted that the company is also not expanding its workforce. “AI allows us to produce more software quicker, but does the over-saturated global software market need a lot more software?” he asked, adding that growth in the sector will be slower as focus shifts to quality and brand.Vembu further argued that while automation makes goods cheaper and more accessible, the challenge is ensuing people have income to afford them.He also pointed to Universal Basic Income (UBI) as one possible solution, referencing Sam Altman’s $14 million investment into UBI research. “Some people think the answer is UBI, and some of that is already happening in India — we call them freebies. We can expect the political pressure to do a lot more. Is there a better answer?” Vembu asked.For those unaware, Sam Altman’s Universal Basic Income (UBI) theory is rooted in the idea that as artificial intelligence and automation eliminate traditional jobs, societies will need a safety net to ensure people can still afford basic necessities. He believes UBI — guaranteed cash payments to all citizens — could be one of the most viable solutions. As CEO of OpenAI, Altman has long warned that AI could displace millions of jobs. He argues that while automation makes goods cheaper, people still need income to buy them. Altman invested $14 million through OpenResearch, alongside $10 million from OpenAI, to run one of the largest UBI trials in the U.S.
Article Summary: Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu has publicly raised concerns about artificial intelligence ‘wiping’ jobs. He warned that India must urgently find answers to safeguard its massive youth workforce. He also pointed to Universal Basic Income (UBI) as one possible solution, referencing Sam Altman’s $14 million investment into UBI research.

Article Title: Top economist Steve Hanke does not agree with Elon Musk on ‘free AI’, calls it ‘disconnect from reality’
Article Text:
‘AI infrastructure demands massive capital and physical resources’



Steve Hanke pushes back on mass automation, job cuts and ‘universal high income’



Prominent economist Steve Hanke has strongly dismissed predictions that artificial intelligence (AI) will eventually become free and universally accessible. He labelled the expectations of “free AI” a delusion driven by flawed economic thinking. Hanke, a professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University and a former senior economist on President Ronald Reagan’s Council of Economic Advisers, warned that the extreme resource requirements of AI infrastructure make zero-cost access impossible.Nontably, his comments directly push back against predictions made by Tesla and xAI CEO Elon Musk , who has argued that AI will usher in an era of post-scarcity abundance where goods and services become virtually free.As per Business Insider, unlike traditional software, which carries near-zero marginal distribution costs once built, generative AI relies on continuous, high-cost physical infrastructure. This includes advanced graphics processing units (GPUs), massive electrical power and millions of gallons of cooling water.“This belief is based on a disconnect from reality, as well as a good dose of idiotic economic reasoning.AI is incredibly costly; it is very resource intensive. It requires huge amounts of water, power, and physical capital,” Hanke said regarding the concept of costless AI.Hanke also criticised tech visionaries who equate AI with legacy software, describing the comparison as “apples and oranges”, while predicting that the finite availability and rising cost of physical resources will ultimately dictate the boundaries and pace of the AI boom.In the meantime, major technology groups, including Microsoft, Google-parent Alphabet, Amazon and Meta have already projected hundreds of billions of dollars in capital expenditures to construct the specialised data centres required to run frontier models.Hanke also rejected claims that AI will trigger immediate, widespread unemployment across the workforce. Elon Musk has previously suggested that AI will automate most jobs, advising that governments will need to implement a “universal high income” to support citizens and suggesting people may no longer need to save for retirement.Hanke countered that replacing human workers with AI will often prove expensive for businesses than retaining human employees, limiting how quickly companies can automate tasks.“Businesses will not be firing everybody and replacing them with AI,” Hanke noted, emphasising that corporate adoption will be constrained by operational costs rather than pure capability.
Article Summary: Economist Steve Hanke has strongly dismissed predictions that artificial intelligence (AI) will eventually become free and universally accessible. He labelled the expectations of “free AI” a delusion driven by flawed economic thinking. Hanke, a professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University, warned that the extreme resource requirements of AI make zero-cost access impossible.

Article Title: Scientists build low-cost AI cameras to protect Bumblebees, petition to list under Endangered Species Act
Article Text:
Scientists build low-cost AI cameras to protect Bumblebees

Technology overcomes traditional survey challenges



Machine learning matches traditional accuracy



Scientists at Oregon State University have developed a low-cost, AI-powered camera system that is capable of monitoring bumblebee populations without relying on lethal traps or expensive, manual field surveys. The research team’s findings, which were published in the journal Remote Sensing in Ecology and Conservation, show that the non-invasive technology could transform insect conservation and agricultural planning at a critical moment. Several bumblebee species face severe population declines and are being evaluated for federal protection under the Endangered Species Act.Historically, tracking pollinator populations required labour-intensive hand-netting or lethal blue-vane traps. While effective at documenting species diversity, traditional traps kill the insects being studied and direct manual observation requires extensive time and financial resources. To solve this, researchers built an affordable camera setup using off-the-shelf commercial components and tested it in a flowering red clover field at Oregon State’s Hyslop Field Research Laboratory in Corvallis.To lure daylight-active (diurnal) insects like bumblebees toward the lenses, the team tested various visual backgrounds.They discovered that placing a bullseye pattern behind the cameras drew significantly more bee visits compared to plain, solid backgrounds.To process thousands of photos automatically, the researchers trained custom deep-learning computer vision models. They found that “tiled" AI models – which slice images into smaller grids to evaluate localized details – outperformed standard models analysing full-frame photos.According to the research results, during field trials, the camera system successfully documented six distinct bumblebee species. The data mirrored the species diversity captured through traditional netting and lethal trapping, proving that remote camera monitoring can deliver accurate data without harming local ecosystems.“Insects are vitally important, and we need methods to better understand their populations. This tool should help us to do that in a low-cost, easily scalable manner,” said Michael Getz, a data scientist at the Biodiversity Research Institute in Maine, who led the project as a master’s student at Oregon State University.The ability to collect large volumes of field data could prove crucial for wildlife agencies and agricultural producers. Many commercial crops rely heavily on native bees for pollination, yet conservationists often lack the widespread population data needed to implement targeted recovery plans.Andony Melathopoulos, an associate professor of pollinator health at Oregon State and co-author of the study, noted that missing data frequently complicates federal decisions regarding endangered species listings and critical habitat designations.“This technology opens up the possibility for much richer data so that we can be more precise when it comes to decisions on listing a species and characterizing critical habitat,” Melathopoulos explained.
Article Summary: Scientists at Oregon State University have developed a low-cost, AI-powered camera system that is capable of monitoring bumblebee populations. The non- invasive technology could transform insect conservation and agricultural planning at a critical moment. Several bumblebees face severe population declines and are being evaluated for federal protection under the Endangered Species Act.

Article Title: Dutch bookseller thought a 3,000-book order was a scam until he learned it may have been for AI
Article Text:
Representative Image

"I was shocked!"

"2077AI,"

Bookseller initially thought the request was a scam

"Very unusual,"

"That's why I regarded the request as spam or phishing."

"They didn't take it seriously"

"considered it as scam,"

"I deal in old and

rare books

,"

"These books are expensive and exclusive. So I do not do bulk trade."

AI companies increasingly seek physical books

Bulk book sourcing draws attention

A Dutch antiquarian bookseller initially dismissed an email requesting more than 3,000 books as a scam. Weeks later, he discovered the unusual order may have been linked to artificial intelligence (AI) training, highlighting how AI companies are increasingly looking beyond the internet for books and other high-quality written material.The request was received by Pieter de Vries, an antiquarian bookseller in Haarlem, Netherlands. Speaking to Fortune, de Vries said he ignored the email until a Dutch journalist contacted him about it.he said after learning of the possible AI connection. The email, sent by someone identifying herself as Natalia from a company calledincluded a spreadsheet containing 3,001 ISBNs and asked booksellers to source the titles, prepare quotations and estimate shipping costs to China.According to Fortune, the spreadsheet listed books published mainly between 2020 and 2021 by academic publishers including Elsevier, Wiley, Routledge, Emerald Publishing and Oxford University Press. The subjects ranged from business and engineering to education, medicine and public policy. De Vries said the size of the request immediately made it appear suspicious.he said.He added that several other Dutch antiquarian booksellers received the same inquiry and dismissed it as well.andde Vries told Fortune. Unlike large secondhand book dealers, de Vries specialises in rare and antiquarian books.he said.Although the email never mentioned AI or explained the purpose of the purchase, it surfaced as AI companies continue to search for high-quality training material beyond publicly available web content.Last year, court documents revealed that Anthropic had purchased millions of physical books, removed their bindings, scanned them and discarded the originals as part of an internal project known as Project Panama, according to The Washington Post.The process, commonly known as destructive scanning, involves cutting the spine off a book so individual pages can be scanned quickly before the physical copy is discarded.The copyright dispute later ended after a US federal judge ruled that using legally purchased books for AI training constituted fair use. Separate claims related to books downloaded from the LibGen and PiLiMi online libraries were later resolved through a settlement.Anthropic has said its Claude AI models are trained using a combination of publicly available web content, commercially acquired datasets and internally generated data. The company also said it purchases books through standard commercial markets and does not acquire or destroy rare or antiquarian books.The report also sheds light on how AI companies may source large quantities of printed books. Earlier this year, 404 Media reported that ISBNdb had advertised services to help AI laboratories purchase between 1,000 and one million printed books for large language model training. The company later told Fortune that the service was never launched and that the webpages reflected only an exploratory concept, not an active business.Similar reports have also emerged from Germany and Switzerland, where secondhand booksellers reportedly received unusually large orders for specialised books. Canadian company Zoom Books, which was mentioned in some reports, denied that the purchases were related to AI training and told Swiss broadcaster SRF that they were part of its regular recycling and book-trading business.
Article Summary: Dutch antiquarian bookseller initially dismissed email requesting more than 3,000 books as a scam. Weeks later, he discovered the unusual order may have been linked to artificial intelligence (AI) training. The email never mentioned AI or explained the purpose of the purchase. It surfaced as AI companies continue to search for high-quality training material.

Article Title: 'Are you interviewing Claude or the person?’: Stanford professor on why tech companies are reviving in-person interviews
Article Text:
Representative Image

"Are you interviewing

Claude

or the person?"

How is AI is changing technical hiring

"A lot of tech firms used to hire folks based on coding tests. They can't do that anymore,"

More employers are returning to in-person interviews

Some companies are embracing AI instead

"The human element of oversight and expertise is more crucial than ever,"

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how technology companies assess job candidates, with many firms bringing applicants back to the office for key interview rounds. According to Stanford economist Nick Bloom, AI tools are making it increasingly difficult for employers to determine whether candidates are demonstrating their own skills during virtual coding interviews.Speaking on the Financial Times' Economics Show podcast, Bloom said many companies no longer fully trust online technical assessments.he said, referring to Anthropic's AI chatbot. According to Bloom, some tech firms have begun conducting middle and final interview rounds in person to reduce the likelihood that candidates rely on AI-generated answers.Bloom said online coding tests, which have long been a common hiring tool for technology companies, are becoming less reliable because candidates can use AI assistants in real time during interviews.Bloom said.According to him, candidates can prompt AI systems during virtual interviews and simply read the generated responses, making it harder for recruiters to accurately evaluate technical ability.Data from recruitment platform Greenhouse indicates that employers are increasingly adding in-person stages to the hiring process.The company's 2025 AI in Hiring Report, based on responses from more than 4,100 job seekers, recruiters and hiring managers across the US, UK, Ireland and Germany, found that 39% of US hiring managers were conducting more in-person interviews to verify candidates' skills.Greenhouse's 2026 AI in Hiring Report, which covered employers in the UK, Ireland and Germany, found the trend continuing, with companies introducing more practical assessments to validate candidates amid concerns over AI-assisted applications and hiring fraud.While some employers are tightening interview processes, others are allowing candidates to use AI tools during assessments. Earlier this year, Google launched a pilot programme allowing software engineering candidates to use an approved AI assistant during interviews. AI-focused startups, including Cognition, Base44, and Replit, have also incorporated AI into their technical hiring processes.Rather than banning AI, some employers are placing greater emphasis on evaluating problem-solving, critical thinking and collaboration alongside technical knowledge.Cisco is among the companies moving away from traditional coding challenges in favour of project-based exercises that assess how candidates work in AI-assisted environments.Scott McGuckin, Cisco's Vice President of Global Talent Acquisition, told Business Insider earlier this month.According to Bloom, AI has changed not only how job candidates are prepared for interview sessions but also how employers verify skills, prompting some technology firms to rethink the balance between virtual and face-to-face hiring.
Article Summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how technology companies assess job candidates. Many firms are bringing applicants back to the office for key interview rounds. AI tools are making it increasingly difficult for employers to determine whether candidates are demonstrating their own skills during virtual coding interviews.

Article Title: As companies battle rising AI costs, EY says its invisible router reduced token use by 60%
Article Text:
Businesses face increasing artificial intelligence costs due to token-based pricing models. EY has implemented an AI router to automatically direct queries to the most suitable models. This system significantly reduces token consumption by directing simpler tasks to less expensive AI. Companies are now shifting focus from AI adoption to monitoring usage and ensuring value. EY's initiative highlights a new phase balancing cost, efficiency, and business outcomes.

"invisible"

"To the users, it makes no apparent change,"

"They open the frontier model, enter their prompt, and get a response. But behind the scenes, the router is deciding where their query should go."

How EY's AI router works

"Many times, it's faster than the frontier models, because to use the heavier models means there's more thinking that gets put in place, and it takes longer to be able to get back to the answer,"

Rising AI token costs become a concern

"A lot of these big bills that companies are getting surprised by are by the top one or the top 2% of people inside the employee base that are just using the wrong tool for the job,"

Companies shift focus from AI adoption to efficiency

"If we ask this question in six months from now, it would probably be like 90% of people,"

Measuring AI beyond costs

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming more expensive for businesses as companies increasingly pay per token rather than with flat-rate subscriptions. To manage those rising costs, one of the Big Four consulting firms, EY, has revealed that it has deployed anAI router that automatically directs employee queries to the most appropriate AI model without changing the user experience.Speaking to Business Insider, Dan Diasio, EY's global consulting AI leader, said the system has reduced AI token consumption by 60% in some divisions since its global rollout in April.Diasio said.Unlike a traditional chatbot, EY's router operates in the background. Instead of sending every request to the most advanced and often most expensive AI model, it analyses the query and routes it to the model best suited for the task.According to Diasio, simpler requests can often be handled by smaller models, which not only cost fewer tokens but also respond faster.he said.The router has been deployed across department-specific AI platforms, including tax and risk functions. It is not used for the Microsoft Copilot chatbot, which is available to all EY employees.The initiative comes as AI providers increasingly shift to token-based pricing, where businesses pay based on the amount of text processed and generated by AI models. Between February and June, companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and GitHub introduced or expanded pricing models linked to token usage.According to EY's latest AI Pulse Survey, 82% of senior leaders at organisations investing in AI said they are concerned about token consumption. The survey was conducted between April and May among 534 senior decision-makers at US companies.Diasio said.Diasio said the first phase of enterprise AI adoption focused on encouraging employees to use AI as much as possible. Companies are now placing greater emphasis on monitoring usage and ensuring that AI spending delivers measurable value.According to the survey, 64% of senior leaders said their organisations already monitor AI token usage and have established budget controls. Diasio expects that number to increase further.he said.EY has also introduced token budgets based on employees' roles and departments. Staff who exceed their allocation can request additional tokens through an approval process.Beyond controlling token usage, Diasio said companies should invest in improving prompts and building stronger internal knowledge systems so AI models can generate more relevant responses using company-specific data.He added that businesses should also evaluate AI by looking beyond direct financial returns.Instead, organisations should ask whether AI helps employees complete work faster and enables them to take on new responsibilities, rather than focusing solely on profit-and-loss metrics.According to Diasio, enterprise AI deployment is entering a new phase in which businesses are increasingly focused on balancing cost, efficiency, and business outcomes.
Article Summary: EY has implemented an AI router to automatically direct queries to the most suitable models. This system significantly reduces token consumption by directing simpler tasks to less expensive AI. Companies are shifting focus from AI adoption to monitoring usage and ensuring value. EY's initiative highlights a new phase balancing cost, efficiency, and business outcomes.

Article Title: Google Gemini to build apps directly as Google scraps AI Studio for Android, iOS
Article Text:
Representative Image

AI Studio app canceled

Gemini to create apps

AI Studio website continues

Implications

Google has canceled its planned AI Studio mobile app for Android and iOS, instead shifting focus to Gemini itself — which will eventually be able to create mobile and desktop apps directly from conversations, according to a report by 9to5Google. The move signals a deeper integration of generative AI into Gemini, positioning it as a platform where apps emerge naturally rather than through separate downloads.At I/O 2026, Google teased an AI Studio app designed to let users capture ideas on the go and turn them into working prototypes. Over 800,000 users pre-ordered the app on Google Play and the App Store, showing strong interest in mobile software creation. However, Google has now confirmed the app will not be released.Instead of launching another standalone app, Google said: “We’ve decided to take an entirely different approach: one where apps emerge naturally, in the course of your everyday conversations with Gemini.”The Gemini team is working on enabling mobile and desktop app creation directly within Gemini, making it possible to generate applications seamlessly during chats.This approach reflects Google’s vision of generative user interfaces (GUIs), where AI builds tools tailored to user needs in real time.For example, Gemini could create a gardening app that teaches basics, tracks plants, and sends reminders — all generated from a simple conversation. While similar functionality exists today via Gemini Canvas and progressive web apps (PWAs), Google aims to deliver a more native experience, especially on Android.Although the mobile app has been scrapped, the AI Studio website will continue to operate for users who want to go from idea to prompt to business. Google emphasised that work on the web platform remains active, while mobile listings have been pulled.* For developers: Gemini could become a direct app-building environment, reducing reliance on separate tools.* For consumers: Everyday conversations with Gemini may produce personalized apps without downloads.* For Google: This strategy strengthens Gemini’s role as a central hub for AI-driven productivity and creativity.
Article Summary: Google has canceled its planned AI Studio mobile app for Android and iOS. The move signals a deeper integration of generative AI into Gemini. Gemini will eventually be able to create mobile and desktop apps directly from conversations. Over 800,000 users pre-ordered the app on Google Play and the App Store.

Article Title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day leaked on X, reached 5.9 million accounts, and then…
Article Text:
5.9 million accounts saw the Spider-Man leak on X. Sony still had a record Friday.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day

The Odyssey last week, Spider-Man this week: How X keeps ending up as the internet's biggest movie leak platform

A high-quality bootleg ofsat in plain sight on X for most of Friday, reaching 5.9 million accounts before Sony managed to get it pulled. The post went up at 6:05 am PT from an account calling itself Fredrick Bryan, early enough that plenty of people in the US saw the film before their local matinee started. It stayed live until roughly 3:25 pm PT, by which point it had collected more than 143,000 likes and over 10,000 reshares.Copies surfaced on other accounts through the day, though most lasted only minutes. Clips spoiling the film's biggest reveals spread faster than the full rip and proved harder to contain, with many of those posts now replaced by a copyright-disabled notice. Sony declined to comment.This is the second time in eight days that a major release has been dumped on X in full. A three-hour rip of Christopher Nolan'swent up last weekend, pulled 2.1 million views in two and a half hours, and ended with the account suspended. Universal said it moved to takedown protocols as soon as it spotted the upload and would chase every remedy available to protect its copyright.The mechanics are simple enough. Since Elon Musk's 2022 rebrand, X Premium subscribers have been able to upload videos up to four hours long, which is comfortably more runway than most tentpoles need.None of it slowed the film down.took $72 million in previews, including Tuesday early-access screenings, beating the $60 millionmanaged in 2019. Friday's opening day landed at roughly $168 million with previews folded in, ahead of's $157.4 million.Sony is guiding conservatively at $325 million for the weekend.'s $357 million still stands as the domestic record, withsecond at $260 million.Tom Holland returns as Peter Parker alongside Zendaya's MJ, with Sadie Sink in a role Sony has worked hard to keep under wraps, plus Jon Bernthal and Jacob Batalon. IGN scored it 7/10.The leak was enormous by any normal measure. It just happened to run into a weekend where several million people paid for a ticket regardless.
Article Summary: 5.9 million accounts saw the Spider-Man leak on X. Sony still had a record Friday. A three-hour rip of Christopher Nolan'swent up last weekend, pulled 2.1 million views in two and a half hours. Universal said it moved to takedown protocols as soon as it spotted the upload.
